classification: allocator high-water retention of virtual address space and clean/reusable pages, not a live-object memory leak
interpretation: The BAML collector reclaimed the request graph: runtime objects fell to 15 and malloc live bytes fell by about 31.2 MiB.
The unchanged 164 MiB malloc reservation is allocator-owned virtual address space retained at its high-water mark.

After GC, vmmap attributed only 24.7 MiB of the malloc zone to dirty pages even though ps-style RSS counted 143.7 MiB resident. The 76 MiB of completely empty MALLOC_SMALL regions was almost entirely clean, so it does not represent 76 MiB of live or dirty process memory.
The remaining dirty allocator fragmentation was about 5.2 MiB, or 21% of dirty malloc-zone bytes; it was bounded and far smaller than the apparent RSS gap.

Maximal malloc_zone_pressure_relief found no additional releasable bytes because the allocator had already made its empty pages reclaimable. Keeping the address mappings and clean pages visible in RSS is not a classical memory leak.

This run did not reproduce the original late reservation step: RSS and malloc reservation were exactly flat for the final 90 loaded seconds. A longer run is still needed to prove a permanent plateau, but the retained floor observed here is allocator high-water behavior rather than unreachable live allocations.
